name: MCP602T-I_SN
title: 2.7 V to 6.0 V single-supply CMOS op amps (MCP601, MCP601R, MCP602, MCP603, MCP604)
summary: A family of low-power CMOS operational amplifiers for one 2.7 V to 6.0 V supply, in single (MCP601, MCP601R), single with chip select (MCP603), dual (MCP602) and quad (MCP604) versions. Each amplifier draws 230 µA typical, has a 2.8 MHz gain bandwidth and 1 pA typical input bias current, is unity-gain stable, swings its output rail to rail and takes inputs from 0.3 V below VSS to 1.2 V below VDD. Industrial (-40 °C to +85 °C) and extended (-40 °C to +125 °C) grades.
key_figures: 230 µA typ, 325 µA max per amplifier
rail to rail, within 15 mV of VSS and 20 mV of VDD (25 kΩ load)

circuits.title: AC and DC test circuit, non-inverting gain
circuits.description: The amplifier is measured with the signal into RN at the non-inverting input and RG returned to VDD/2; RF closes the loop and CL with RL (to VL) load the output. The supply has 0.1 µF from VDD to VSS and 1 µF from VDD to ground.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

circuits.title: AC and DC test circuit, inverting gain
circuits.description: The amplifier is measured with VDD/2 into RN at the non-inverting input and the signal into RG at the inverting input; RF closes the loop and CL with RL (to VL) load the output. The supply has 0.1 µF from VDD to VSS and 1 µF from VDD to ground.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

circuits.title: Protecting the analog inputs
circuits.description: R1 and R2 sit in series with the two inputs and limit the current that can be pulled out of them when V1 or V2 swings below VSS, where the internal ESD diodes conduct. D1 and D2 run from each input pin to VDD and carry any overvoltage current into the supply; R1 and R2 also limit that current. R3 is the feedback resistor from the output to the inverting input.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

notes: D1 and D2 may instead go on the source side of R1 and R2; their current must then be limited some other way, and the resistors act as in-rush limiters.

circuits.title: Unity-gain buffer
circuits.description: The output drives the inverting input directly, so the output equals the input. Because the output is also the inverting input's common-mode voltage, it has to stay below VDD - 1.2 V for the amplifier to work correctly.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

circuits.title: Series output resistor RISO for a large capacitive load
circuits.description: A non-inverting stage set by RF and RG drives a capacitive load CL through RISO. The resistor makes the load look resistive at high frequency, which restores phase margin; the feedback is taken at the amplifier pin, ahead of RISO. Pick RISO from the recommended-RISO curve against CL/GN.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

circuits.title: Unused amplifier, circuit A: buffered reference
circuits.description: A spare amplifier of the MCP604 is wired as a follower of the R1/R2 divider from VDD. It sits at its minimum noise gain and its output holds VREF = VDD × R2 / (R1 + R2), any level inside the output range, instead of toggling and coupling into the other channels.

circuits.title: Unused amplifier, circuit B: comparator
circuits.description: The fewest parts: the non-inverting input goes to VDD and the inverting input to VSS, so the spare amplifier works as a comparator with its output parked at one rail. It can draw more supply current than circuit A.

circuits.title: Second-order low-pass Sallen-Key filter, 10 Hz
circuits.description: A unity-gain (G = +1 V/V) second-order Butterworth low-pass with a 10 Hz cutoff. R1 and R2 feed the non-inverting input with C2 to ground; C1 returns the output to the R1/R2 junction. The very low input bias current lets the resistors be large and the capacitors small.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

circuits.title: Second-order low-pass multiple-feedback filter, 10 Hz
circuits.description: An inverting (G = -1 V/V) second-order Butterworth low-pass with a 10 Hz cutoff. R1 brings the input to a node with C2 to ground; R2 feeds back from the output to that node and R3 carries it on to the inverting input, which C1 ties to the output. The non-inverting input sits at VDD/2.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

circuits.title: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier
circuits.description: Two input amplifiers, each a follower of V1 or V2 with gain set by its R2 and the shared RG, drive a difference stage (R3, R4) whose reference end goes to VREF. VOUT = (V1 - V2)(1 + 2R2/RG)(R4/R3) + VREF. Unity gain is possible; the common-mode input range narrows as R2/RG grows. CMRR depends on the op amp CMRR and on resistor matching; a bulk bypass capacitor of 1 µF or more is called for.

circuits.title: Two-op-amp instrumentation amplifier
circuits.description: The first amplifier takes V2 and, with R1 from VREF and R2 in feedback, drives the second through another R2; the second amplifier takes V1 and has R1 in feedback, and RG joins the two inverting inputs. VOUT = (V1 - V2)(1 + R1/R2 + 2R1/RG) + VREF. It uses less power than the three-amplifier version, but its common-mode range shrinks at higher gain and the gain must be 2 or more. CMRR depends on the op amp CMRR and on resistor matching; a bulk bypass capacitor of 1 µF or more is called for.

circuits.title: Photovoltaic-mode photodiode detector
circuits.description: A transimpedance amplifier: the photodiode D1 sits between the inverting input and ground with no voltage across it, and its current ID1 flows through R2 to give VOUT = ID1 × R2. Zero bias gives the best light sensitivity and linearity, suited to precision work; it relies on low bias current and low noise at the input, a common-mode range that includes ground and a rail-to-rail output. C2 across R2 is optional and can help stability.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

circuits.title: Photoconductive-mode photodiode detector
circuits.description: A transimpedance amplifier with the photodiode D1 reverse-biased from VBIAS (below 0 V) to the inverting input; VOUT = ID1 × R2. The reverse bias lowers the diode capacitance for faster response, at the price of more leakage current and linearity error, and asks for a wide gain bandwidth. C2 across R2 is optional and can help stability.

parts.note: any single amplifier of the family

notes: VBIAS < 0V.

operation.text: Low-power CMOS op amps for one supply of 2.7 V to 6.0 V: MCP601 single, MCP601R single with a rotated SOT-23-5 pinout, MCP602 dual, MCP603 single with chip select, MCP604 quad. Each draws 230 µA (typ) per amplifier, has a 2.8 MHz gain bandwidth, is stable at unity gain, swings its output to the rails and accepts inputs down to 0.3 V below ground. I parts are specified from -40°C to +85°C and E parts from -40°C to +125°C. MCP602T-I/SN is the dual, industrial range, 8-lead SOIC, on tape and reel.

MCP601, MCP602 and MCP603 come in 8-lead PDIP, SOIC and TSSOP. MCP601 and MCP601R also come in 5-lead SOT-23 (MCP601R only in that package), MCP603 in 6-lead SOT-23, and MCP604 in 14-lead PDIP, SOIC and TSSOP.

VDD sits 2.7 V to 6.0 V above VSS (one pin description gives 2.5 V, a misprint for 2.7 V), and the other pins stay between the two rails in normal use. In single-supply use VSS is ground. VDD needs bypassing: a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF capacitor within 2 mm of the pin for high-frequency performance and a bulk capacitor of 1 µF or more within 100 mm for large slow currents; neighbouring analog parts may share the bulk capacitor.

Each input has ESD diodes that guard the input transistors while keeping bias current low. They clamp an input that falls a diode drop or more under VSS, and break down above VDD at a level high enough for normal operation yet low enough to divert fast ESD events. The surrounding circuit must hold the input pin currents and voltages within the absolute maximum ratings; series resistors R1 and R2 limit the current drawn out of the pins below ground, and external diodes D1 and D2 to VDD keep the pins from rising too far above the supply. With the common-mode voltage below VSS the inputs can source a large current, so high-impedance sources may need a narrower usable range.
Driving the inputs past the supply rails does not invert the output; it simply limits at the rail.

The input stage is linear for VCM from VSS - 0.3 V to VDD - 1.2 V at +25°C: the range includes ground but not VDD. In a unity-gain follower the output is the inverting input, so the output must stay below VDD - 1.2 V.

Two figures describe swing. Maximum output voltage swing is the furthest the output can be driven under the stated load, for example within 15 mV of the negative rail with 25 kΩ to VDD/2. Linear output voltage swing is how far it goes while still in its linear region; it is checked by measuring large-signal AOL 100 mV inside each rail, and has to reach the specified AOL minimum.

Pulling CS high drops the supply current to -0.7 µA (typ), drawn through the CS pin to VSS, and the output goes to high impedance; a low level on CS turns the amplifier on. An internal 5 MΩ (typ) pull-down to VSS enables the part when CS floats. The switch has 0.4 V of hysteresis at VDD = 5.0 V; turn-on takes 3.1 µs typ (10 µs max) and turn-off 100 ns typ.

A large capacitive load erodes phase margin and bandwidth, which shows as peaking in the frequency response and overshoot and ringing on steps. Above about 40 pF at G = +1, a small series resistor RISO between the output and the load restores margin by making the load resistive at high frequency; the bandwidth is then usually lower than without the load. RISO is chosen from the recommended-RISO curve against CL/GN, then the peaking and overshoot are checked on the bench or with the SPICE macro model and RISO adjusted.

A spare amplifier in the MCP604 is tied off so its output cannot toggle and cause crosstalk: either as a follower of a resistor divider (circuit A, minimum noise gain, any reference inside the output range) or as a comparator with its inputs to the rails (circuit B, fewest parts, possibly more supply current).

operation.topic: PCB surface leakage and guard rings
operation.text: Humidity, dust and contamination make the board leak; about 10^12 Ω between nearby traces in dry conditions, which at 5 V gives 5 pA, above the 1 pA typical bias current. A guard ring around the sensitive pins, held at their voltage, cuts this. For non-inverting stages, unity-gain followers included, the ring goes to VIN- (the common-mode voltage); for inverting and transimpedance stages it goes to VIN+, the reference such as VDD/2 or ground.

The two filter circuits are 10 Hz second-order Butterworth low-pass designs, a Sallen-Key with gain +1 V/V and a multiple-feedback with gain -1 V/V. The low bias current permits large resistors and small capacitors, which keeps the layout compact.
